definition: A contiguous sequence of n items (typically words or characters) from a given text, used in classical statistical language models.
details: N-gram language models, which estimate the probability of a word based on the preceding n-1 words, were the dominant approach to language modeling before neural network-based methods became practical and superior.

explainer.lead: An n-gram is a contiguous sequence of n items, typically words or characters, from a given text, used in classical statistical language models. It matters as the dominant language-modeling approach before neural methods became practical and superior.

tiers.eli5: If you always read words in clumps of three, each clump is a 3-gram — a fixed-size sliding window over the sentence.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers count n-gram frequencies to estimate next-word probabilities and build baselines or spell-checkers. A pitfall is that n-gram tables grow explosively with vocabulary and n, and unseen sequences get zero probability without smoothing.
tiers.paperLevel: Estimates the probability of a word from the preceding n-1 words, p(w_t | w_{t-n+1} ... w_{t-1}). Context is limited to n-1 words, so longer-range dependencies are not captured.

explainer.example: With n=2, a bigram model estimates the next word using only the single preceding word.
